The 265 s serial group costs the same on 4 cores and 18
maxWorkers=4 is a cheap CI proxy

label: Both suites run on ubuntu-latest with job timeouts of 51 and 34 minutes and no shard matrix, so the smaller runner is GitHub's default host rather than a self-hosted machine.

CI already runs upgrade-legacy.vitest.ts in its own background process beside the rest of the cli files and joins them with wait, so sharding that file is a test change inside the existing process, not a workflow change.

The core lane's parallel efficiency is poor, about 1.3-1.4x and possibly close to 1.0x, comparing roughly 302 s of summed import plus test time against a 348-399 s wall, which predicts a four-core runner costs about the same wall rather than more.

The deep-loop suite's 265 s serial group is the one cost identical on eighteen cores and on four, because it never uses more than one worker, which makes shrinking it the highest-value cut for a smaller runner.
--maxWorkers=4 is the cheap CI proxy: neither config pins maxWorkers and Vitest accepts the flag, so one four-worker run on this Mac predicts the ubuntu-latest wall without provisioning a runner.

The ranking is: shrink the serial group first because it is core-count independent, split heavy files second because it shortens every runner's critical path, cut summed import work third because it is worth about 17 s at eighteen cores, and drop ledger caching because it buys nothing on the append path.

direction: A CI shard matrix as the first move
reason: Both jobs fit their timeouts and sharding multiplies setup and build cost before any file is faster
The measured machine is not the machine that gates merges

direction: Treating summed import work as the small-runner lever
reason: It becomes material only below a handful of cores and the serial group dominates first

label: No CI timing history is checked in, so the ubuntu-latest wall for either suite is unknown and the four-worker proxy is the only estimate available from this repository
